lines.text: You've found all thirteen devices on the robot. Now Tuner X measures the drivetrain and writes one file about it, so get the robot up on blocks first.
The generator would happily write a whole project. You don't need one. Yours is already written, and all it's missing is the numbers for your robot.
Start with the device list: thirteen devices on one bus, no two sharing an ID. Write them down by corner, because the wizard asks which ones sit where.
Then four numbers, off a tape measure and not the CAD. Both distances run between module centers.
Each corner gets its encoder and two motors, then a calibration with the wheel straight. If a different corner moves during the checks, its devices are assigned to the wrong module.
Slow down here. Generate only the constants, not a project, and put that file over the one already in yours. The team number is the only other edit.
Keep a hand on disable. Enabled with nobody touching the controller, nothing should move. On the floor, turn the robot ninety degrees and push forward, and it should head the same way as before.
No robot yet? Plain simulation runs the same code with no hardware at all, and later swerve lessons lean on it.
Three files make the drivetrain, and two are Tuner X's. The third is written by hand, and it's the one your OpModes talk to.
Remember that a canceled command leaves its last request in the motors. For a drivetrain that's a speed, so the robot would keep rolling.
So the drivetrain gets a default command that reads the sticks every loop. Let go and it's still running, just asking for zero. It's set in the robot, not an OpMode, so every mode has it.
The left bumper makes wherever the robot faces now the new forward. The numbers in your new file are only a starting point, though, and tuning them comes next.
